sections.heading: Objects
sections.summary: In computer science an object can be almost anything in a programmatic sense: a variable, a data model, a function, a class, or a method. In object-oriented programming (OOP) an object is an instance that usually represents a real-world thing. It has properties (characteristics), behaviors (methods), and states (data).
common_mistakes: The slide says an object has properties, behaviors, and states. Wrong choices on the quiz were "functions and loops only", "inputs and outputs only", and "hardware and network devices".

memory_aids.label: Objects
memory_aids.text: An object = P-B-S: Properties, Behaviors, States. Say it as "Pretty Big Spoons".

sections.heading: Object-Oriented Analysis (OOA)
sections.summary:
OOA is an iterative stage of analysis during the software development life cycle. It models the functional requirements of the software while staying completely independent of any implementation requirements. It looks at everything through the lens of objects and combines behaviors, characteristics, and states into one analysis process instead of splitting them into separate stages.

The Five Activities Of OOA:
• Find and define the objects.
• Organize the objects.
• Describe how the objects interact with one another.
• Define the external behavior of the objects.
• Define the internal behavior of the objects.

memory_aids.label: The Five Activities Of OOA
memory_aids.text:
Fast Owls Do Eat Insects = Find, Organize, Describe interactions, External behavior, Internal behavior.
Chunk it as 2 + 1 + 2: objects (1 and 2), interaction (3), behavior outside then inside (4 and 5).

sections.heading: Object-Oriented Design (OOD)
sections.summary: OOD is an extension of OOA. The difference is that it considers implementation constraints. An analyzed object or object model has to be designed and implemented for real, which usually needs constraints such as software or hardware platforms, time and budget limits, performance requirements, and developer aptitude.

memory_aids.label: Object-Oriented Design (OOD)
memory_aids.text: A = Analyze what, D = Design how. If a quiz option says OOD "eliminates the identified objects" or "avoids software and hardware requirements", it is wrong: OOD keeps the objects and adds the constraints.

comparisons.title: Object-Oriented Design (OOD)
rows: How will it be built under real limits?
The analyzed objects plus implementation constraints
Considers it (platform, time, budget, performance, skills)

sections.heading: Object-Oriented Analysis And Design (OOAD)
sections.summary: OOAD is a technical method of analyzing and designing an application based on the system's object models (the logical components of the system that interact with one another). Development is normally split into loose, abstract stages. The limits of those stages, together with the strict step-by-step staging of the waterfall model, led to the rise of iterative models like OOAD.
common_mistakes: OOAD is a method based on object models. It is not a programming language for databases, not only a testing technique, and not a model for managing computer networks.

memory_aids.label: Advantages And Disadvantages Of OOAD
memory_aids.text: 2 good + 2 bad: Encapsulation and Easy are the good ones (E, E). Ill-suited and Too complex are the bad ones (I, T). "Easy Eggs, Ill Tummies."

comparisons.title: Advantages And Disadvantages Of OOAD
rows: Everything revolves around objects, so systems are truly independent and self-contained. Objects can be mixed and matched as needed.
Based on real-world objects, so everyone on the team (and customers or non-technical users) quickly understands what an object name or behavior means.
Hard to apply OOAD in a procedural language or to non-object business logic. Procedural apps focus on scope and modularity; OO apps focus on objects that simulate the real world.
The simpler the needs, the more likely a less-structured procedural approach is the better fit.

sections.heading: What Procedural Programming Is
sections.summary:
Procedural programming uses a list of instructions that tell the computer what to do step by step. It relies on procedures (routines or subroutines), and each procedure holds a series of computational steps. It is also called imperative programming, and procedural languages are known as top-down languages. It is intuitive because it looks like how you would expect a program to work.

Before OOP became popular, the most common approach was procedural, or structured, programming. Structured programming uses top-down design: it breaks a problem into a series of more and more specific functions. It needs well-defined flow control. Development starts by identifying the problem domain and then defining a top-level function, which is split into more specific procedures.

Grouping separate tasks and finishing them one after another until the larger task is complete.
The mechanism for passing parameters to functions, subroutines, or procedures. Five ways: pass by value, reference, result, value-result, and name.

sections.heading: Module 5, Chapter 3: Methodologies And The System Development Process
sections.summary: A system development methodology is the set of steps used to form, plan, and control the process of developing an information system. It gives guidelines for every activity in system development and includes specific models, tools, and techniques. The word process is a synonym for methodology, and the process is supported by documentation. The chapter cover diagram is the Microsoft Solutions Framework (MSF), a circular model with five phases, each ending in a milestone.

memory_aids.label: Module 5, Chapter 3: Methodologies And The System Development Process
memory_aids.text: MSF phases: E-P-D-S-D = Envision, Plan, Develop, Stabilize, Deploy ("Every Panda Dances, Sleeps, Dreams"). Milestones in the same order: Vision, Plan, Scope, Release, Deployment.

comparisons.title: Module 5, Chapter 3: Methodologies And The System Development Process

sections.heading: The Nine Criteria For Comparing Methodologies
sections.summary: The Nine Criteria For Comparing Methodologies: key points are below.

memory_aids.label: The Nine Criteria For Comparing Methodologies
memory_aids.text:
Chunk 4 + 1 + 3 + 1: the project basics (Process, Product, Cost, Completion date), then Responsiveness, then the people three (Team, Management, Training), then Probability of success.
First four: "Pretty Pandas Cook Cakes."

comparisons.title: The Nine Criteria For Comparing Methodologies
rows: Does the methodology assume every step is well known with no room for change, or is it flexible in all stages?
Is the final product defined early in planning, or during the project and close to closure?
At what stage is the cost estimated?
Is the schedule of deliverables estimated up front or as the project progresses?
How much flexibility is allowed for changes in environment, technology, competition, and others?
Do predefined linear steps block creativity? Does it allow teamwork and interaction?
Is management an obstacle, or does it empower the team by removing obstacles?
Does the methodology allow training and knowledge transfer, or limit what a member can do and learn?
How likely is success given a certain degree of complexity and unpredictability?

sections.heading: The Six System Development Models
sections.summary: The slide lists six models: Waterfall, Iterative, DevOps, V-Model, Spiral, and Prototyping.
common_mistakes: Iterative vs Agile: both deliver in increments, but iterative has fixed increment scope and less customer involvement. V-Model vs Waterfall: V-Model pairs every build stage with a test stage. Waterfall tests only after implementation.

Correct: "flexibility than it offers" and "Businesses that are not sure". (The slides say "flexibility that what it offers" and "Business that aren't sure".) The prototyping diagram feeds refinement back into the prototype build, which is what the loop means.

memory_aids.label: The Six System Development Models
memory_aids.text: W-I-D-V-S-P: "Wise Ice Dragons Vanish Silently, Perhaps."

memory_aids.label: The Six System Development Models
memory_aids.text:
One-line hooks: Waterfall = rigid, requirements first. Iterative = small repeated increments. DevOps = Dev + Ops, continuous delivery. V-Model = waterfall bent up, test every stage. Spiral = risk-driven. Prototyping = early model, feedback.
Spiral quadrants: O-R-D-P = Objectives, Risks, Develop and test, Plan next ("Our Rabbits Dance Politely").

comparisons.title: The Six System Development Models
rows: One of the oldest SDLC models. Rigid structure: all requirements defined at the very start, then design and development. Testing against the original requirements comes after development, then rework.
Out of favor in recent years, but strong for certain projects, especially government contractors.
Stages cascade down: Requirements (product requirements document), Design (software architecture), Implementation (software), Verification, Maintenance.
Takes waterfall and cycles it several times in small increments. Each step becomes several mini-projects that add value as the product evolves.
Shares many goals with agile, but external customers are less involved and the scope of each increment is normally fixed.
Loop through planning, requirements, design, implementation, verification, evaluation. Entry: initialization and planning. Exit: implementation then deployment.
One of the newest methodologies. Combines software Development and IT Operations to shorten the SDLC and give continuous delivery with high software quality.
Brings development and operations teams together to streamline delivery and support. Changes become more fluid and organizational risk drops. Needs flexible resources.
Venn diagram: DevOps sits where Development, QA, and Operations overlap.
An evolution of the classic waterfall. The steps are flipped upwards after the coding phase. Very strict: the next phase starts only when the previous is complete.
Inflexible and higher risk, not recommended for small projects, but easier to manage and control. Good where requirements are static and clearly stated and early testing is wanted.

Left side down: Concept of Operations, Requirements and Architecture, Detailed Design. Bottom: Implementation. Right side up: Integration/Test/Verification, System Verification and Validation, Operation and Maintenance.
Lets teams adopt multiple SDLC models based on the risk patterns of the project. A blend of iterative and waterfall.
The challenge is knowing when to move on to the next phase. Good for businesses unsure of requirements or expecting major edits in mid to high-risk projects.
Four quadrants: 1 Determine objectives, 2 Identify and resolve risks, 3 Development and test, 4 Plan the next iteration. Radius = cumulative cost.
Build an early model of the new system. It has limited functionality and is not thoroughly tested, but gives customers a sense of what is coming.
Feedback is gathered and used through the rest of the SDLC. Works well for emerging industries or new technologies.
Requirements, quick design, build prototype, user evaluation (loops with refining the prototype), implement and maintain.

sections.heading: Module 6, Chapter 1: Software Development Strategies
sections.summary: This chapter is about choosing a development strategy, not about one perfect method. The slides list the reasons to choose carefully, and warn against the most common mistake.

sections.heading: Why Strategy Matters
sections.summary:
• Keep up with the rapidly evolving industry.
• Develop software realistically.
• Consider that every project and team is unique.
• Find the right solution.
• Identify useful techniques relevant to the situation.
• Choose the appropriate development model.

memory_aids.label: Why Strategy Matters
memory_aids.text: Six verbs: Keep up, Be realistic, Remember uniqueness, Find, Identify, Choose. The last three are the decision path: find the solution, pick techniques, choose the model.

sections.heading: The Big Ideas
sections.summary: The Big Ideas: key points are below.

memory_aids.label: The Big Ideas
memory_aids.text: One sentence for the chapter: "No one-size-fits-all: understand the problem, test the plan, keep it flexible." If an option says one methodology guarantees success, it is the trap.

comparisons.title: The Big Ideas
rows: Adopting some methodology does not guarantee a project's success over another methodology or over no single strategy at all.
Assuming what worked in one case will automatically work in another. Common in the software industry and with misunderstood concepts like agile.
Most teams are not industry experts. Most projects do not use groundbreaking tools. They have budgets and timelines and often must interface with less-than-ideal legacy systems.
Adopting a way of doing things because it looks good, without understanding how and why, often ends in disaster.
Applying a one-size-fits-all approach without enough analysis of the specific goals, problems, challenges, and exceptions.
Only a properly evaluated situation, with solutions thoroughly tested and sanity-checked. Otherwise there is no real evidence things will go well.
Pick tools and techniques from each process, as long as you learn what they mean and whether they are compatible and make sense.
There is no "one" perfect solution, but the best possible one for the given problem can be found.

Often works: base it on a thorough understanding of the problem and the shortcomings of known methods, using a toolbox of abstractions and generalizations to re-assemble a strategy from proven components.
High trust and autonomy across the board.
A model or methodology must have flexibility built in, or things pile up the moment anything goes wrong.

sections.heading: Module 6, Chapter 2: Unified Modeling Language (UML)
sections.summary: UML is a general-purpose, developmental modeling language in software engineering, intended to give a standard way to visualize the design of a system. It prescribes a standard set of diagrams and notations for modeling object-oriented systems and describes what the diagrams and symbols mean. It is also used to document business processes and workflows, and some types can replace flowcharts with a more standardized way of modeling and more features for readability.

comparisons.title: Forward Design And Backward Design
rows: Gives a better view of the system or workflow, reveals design issues and flaws, and improves project health.

sections.heading: AI-Native Software Engineering
sections.summary: AI-Native Software Engineering means building software systems where AI is a core part of the design, development, and operation, not just an added feature. It integrates AI models directly into the SDLC, helping systems learn, adapt, and improve automatically.
common_mistakes: Correct: Kubeflow runs on Kubernetes. (The slide spells it "Kubemeters".)

Tools = B-M-O-A: Build/train (TensorFlow, PyTorch), Manage lifecycle (MLflow), Orchestrate (Kubeflow), Assist coding (Copilot).

sections.heading: Maximizing Talent Density
sections.summary: Talent density measures the proportion of high-performing individuals within a workforce. It focuses on quality over quantity.

Measures = P-S-E-R: Performance reviews, Skills assessment, Engagement surveys, Retention and promotion.

comparisons.title: Maximizing Talent Density
rows: 1. Strategic hiring: recruit top performers who match company values and goals.
1. Performance reviews and feedback: show strengths and areas to improve.
2. Employee development: training and mentorship for continuous growth.
2. Skills assessment and benchmarking: identify top performers and skill gaps against standards.
3. Culture of excellence: accountability and high performance.
3. Engagement and satisfaction surveys: measure engagement and alignment.
4. Managing underperformance: constructive feedback and tough decisions.
4. Retention and promotion metrics: track retention and promotion of high performers.

Interoperability, community engagement, and responsible governance.

sections.heading: Green Software Engineering
sections.summary: Green Software Engineering focuses on designing software to minimize environmental impact and promote sustainability. It does not aim to increase environmental impact.

memory_aids.label: Green Software Engineering
memory_aids.text:
Practices = A-O-P-S: Algorithms, Optimize, Profile, Scalable ("Always Open Pretty Skies").
Applications = C-E-E-S: Carbon-aware cloud, Energy-efficient AI, Energy-saving mobile, Sustainable development.

comparisons.title: Green Software Engineering
rows: Lower computational complexity and memory use, so lower energy use.
Optimizing loops and avoiding unnecessary computation decreases power use.
Profiling and benchmarking find performance issues for targeted improvements.
Efficient resource use under varying loads.

comparisons.title: Green Software Engineering
rows: Adjust workloads based on carbon intensity to optimize resources and cut emissions.
Green AI improves training efficiency using optimized hardware and algorithms.
Use less battery and extend device lifespan.
Improves operational efficiency and stakeholder engagement.

cram_sheet.remember: Properties, behaviors, states
Models functional requirements with objects, independent of implementation. Five activities: Find, Organize, Describe interactions, External behavior, Internal behavior
Extends OOA and adds implementation constraints (platform, time, budget, performance, skills)
Method based on a system's object models. Good: encapsulation, easy to understand. Bad: ill-suited to procedural apps, too complex for simple apps
Step-by-step instructions, top-down, imperative. Data exposed to the whole program. Parameter passing: value, reference, result, value-result, name
Functions vs objects, top-down vs bottom-up, no access specifiers vs private/public/protected, no data hiding vs data hiding
Steps to form, plan, and control system development. Nine criteria. Tools (language, IDE, CASE) and techniques (best practices)
Waterfall, Iterative, DevOps, V-Model, Spiral, Prototyping
Rigid requirements first / waterfall bent up with testing pairs / risk-driven in four quadrants
Small fixed-scope increments, less customer involvement / Dev + Ops continuous delivery / early model with feedback
No one-size-fits-all. A methodology does not guarantee success. Build in flexibility
Standard way to visualize system design. Forward = before coding, backward = after coding
Activity, Use case, Timing, State machine, Sequence, Communication
Class, Object, Component, Deployment
AI is core to design, development, and operation. Four key ideas: design, learning, automation, ethics
TensorFlow and PyTorch (build), MLflow (lifecycle), Kubeflow (pipelines), GitHub Copilot (coding)
Large Language Models: trained on large datasets to understand and generate human-like language
LLMs, APIs (integrate with external tools and services), data pipelines
Proportion of high performers; quality over quantity
Shares models, datasets, and tools. Components: models, tools, hosting. Success: interoperability, community, governance
Minimize environmental impact: efficient algorithms, optimization, profiling, scalable code
